lead: A bevel gear pair transmits power between shafts whose axes meet, usually at 90°. The teeth lie on a cone, so tooth size changes from the outer end to the apex. Design converts each cone into an equivalent spur gear on the back cone, then applies the Lewis and Buckingham equations at the mean section where the load acts. You meet this in a hand drill, a vehicle differential and a right-angle gearbox. The aim is to size teeth and face width without using the large-end dimensions for load.
prereq: You need: Lewis and Buckingham from Chapter 7.3 and basic trigonometry (tan, sin, cos).

blocks.text: In a bevel pair the two pitch cones roll on each other without slip. The pitch cone angle γ<sub>1</sub> of the pinion is the half-angle of its pitch cone measured from the shaft axis; γ<sub>2</sub> is the same for the gear. The shaft angle Σ is the angle between the two axes. For Σ = 90°, tan γ<sub>1</sub> = z<sub>1</sub>/z<sub>2</sub> and γ<sub>2</sub> = 90° − γ<sub>1</sub>. The cone angles add to Σ, not to 180°.

Cone distance R is the slant length from the pitch cone apex to the large end. For a 90° pair, R = √((d<sub>1</sub>/2)² + (d<sub>2</sub>/2)²), where d<sub>1</sub> and d<sub>2</sub> are the pitch diameters at the large end. In general R = d<sub>1</sub>/(2 sin γ<sub>1</sub>). The face width b is the tooth length measured along the cone. Keep b ≤ R/3; a wider face twists under load and does not share load evenly.

Dimensions are given at the large end, called the back or crown. Addendum and dedendum are measured there on the back cone, not along the shaft. Because the tooth tapers, the tooth at the small end is smaller. For strength, use the section at the middle of the face, the mean section.

Virtual teeth: unroll the back cone into a plane. The tooth then looks like a spur tooth on a larger circle. Its number is z<sub>v</sub> = z / cos γ for each gear. Use z<sub>v</sub> in the Lewis form factor. Spiral bevel gears have curved teeth and run quieter; hypoid gears have offset axes.

Torque is carried at the mean radius, not the outer radius. The mean cone distance is R<sub>m</sub> = R − b/2. The mean radius of the pinion is r<sub>m1</sub> = R<sub>m</sub> sin γ<sub>1</sub>, also r<sub>m1</sub> = (d<sub>1</sub>/2)(R<sub>m</sub>/R). The mean module is m<sub>m</sub> = m R<sub>m</sub>/R, where m is the module at the large end. For the gear use the same R<sub>m</sub> and its own cone angle.
The tangential force at the mean radius is W<sub>t</sub> = 2T / r<sub>m</sub>, with T in N·mm and r<sub>m</sub> in mm. For power P in kW and speed N in rev/min, T = 60×10<sup>6</sup> P / (2π N) N·mm.

blocks.where: σ is bending stress (N/mm²), W<sub>t</sub> is tangential force at the mean radius (N), b is face width (mm), m<sub>m</sub> is mean module (mm), and Y is the Lewis form factor for z<sub>v</sub>.

blocks.text: Buckingham adds dynamic load: W<sub>d</sub> = W<sub>t</sub> + 21 v (b C + W<sub>t</sub>) / (21 v + √(b C + W<sub>t</sub>)). Here v is pitch-line velocity at the mean radius in m/s, b is face width in mm, C is the deformation factor in N/mm², and W<sub>t</sub>, W<sub>d</sub> are in N.

Straight bevel teeth also produce axial thrust. For pressure angle φ, W<sub>a</sub> ≈ W<sub>t</sub> tan φ sin γ and radial force W<sub>r</sub> ≈ W<sub>t</sub> tan φ cos γ. The thrust goes into the bearings; see Unit 5.

items: Fix the ratio i = z<sub>2</sub>/z<sub>1</sub> and choose z<sub>1</sub> above the undercut limit for the virtual tooth count. Choose the large-end module m from the standard series.

Compute γ<sub>1</sub> = tan⁻¹(z<sub>1</sub>/z<sub>2</sub>), γ<sub>2</sub> = 90° − γ<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>1</sub> = m z<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub> = m z<sub>2</sub> and R = √((d<sub>1</sub>/2)² + (d<sub>2</sub>/2)²). Take b ≤ R/3.
Compute R<sub>m</sub> = R − b/2, m<sub>m</sub> = m R<sub>m</sub>/R, r<sub>m</sub> = R<sub>m</sub> sin γ<sub>1</sub> and W<sub>t</sub> = 2T/r<sub>m</sub>.
Read Y for z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos γ. Use σ = W<sub>t</sub>/(b m<sub>m</sub> Y) to size b or m<sub>m</sub>. Change the trial value until σ is below the allowable stress.

Compute W<sub>d</sub> by Buckingham at the mean velocity v = π d<sub>m</sub> n / 60000, where d<sub>m</sub> is the mean pitch diameter in mm, n is in rev/min, and v is in m/s. Check the tooth for W<sub>d</sub> and for wear.
Compute W<sub>a</sub> and W<sub>r</sub> and give them to the bearing design in Unit 5.

figure.caption: The tree lists the 90° pair in the worked example: pinion and gear cone angles, cone distance and virtual teeth. Notice that the cone angles add to 90°, not 180°.

spec.aria: A tree shows the pinion cone angle 26.57°, gear cone angle 63.43°, cone distance 89.44 mm and virtual teeth 22.36 for a 90° bevel pair.

examples.question: A 90° straight bevel pair has z<sub>1</sub> = 20, z<sub>2</sub> = 40, module 4 mm at the large end and face width 30 mm. Find d<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub>, γ<sub>1</sub>, γ<sub>2</sub>, R, the mean cone distance, the mean module and the pinion virtual teeth.
steps: Large-end pitch diameters: d<sub>1</sub> = m z<sub>1</sub> = 4 × 20 = 80 mm; d<sub>2</sub> = m z<sub>2</sub> = 4 × 40 = 160 mm.
Pinion cone angle: tan γ<sub>1</sub> = z<sub>1</sub>/z<sub>2</sub> = 20/40 = 0.5, so γ<sub>1</sub> = 26.565°. Gear cone angle: γ<sub>2</sub> = 90° − 26.565° = 63.435°.

Mean cone distance: R<sub>m</sub> = R − b/2 = 89.44 − 30/2 = 89.44 − 15 = 74.44 mm. R/3 = 89.44/3 = 29.81 mm, so b = 30 mm is just over the limit (or use b = 29 mm); the example keeps 30 mm for round numbers.
Mean module: m<sub>m</sub> = m R<sub>m</sub>/R = 4 × 74.44/89.44 = 3.33 mm.
Pinion virtual teeth: z<sub>v1</sub> = z<sub>1</sub>/cos γ<sub>1</sub> = 20/cos 26.565° = 20/0.8944 = 22.36.
examples.answer: d<sub>1</sub> = 80 mm, d<sub>2</sub> = 160 mm, γ<sub>1</sub> = 26.57°, γ<sub>2</sub> = 63.43°, R = 89.44 mm, R<sub>m</sub> = 74.44 mm, m<sub>m</sub> = 3.33 mm and z<sub>v1</sub> = 22.36.
examples.check:
import math
z1 = 20
z2 = 40
m = 4.0
b = 30.0
d1 = m * z1
d2 = m * z2
gamma1 = math.degrees(math.atan(z1 / z2))
gamma2 = 90.0 - gamma1
R = math.sqrt((d1/2)**2 + (d2/2)**2)
Rm = R - b/2
mm = m * Rm / R
zv1 = z1 / math.cos(math.radians(gamma1))
print(round(d1, 2))
print(round(d2, 2))
print(round(gamma1, 2))
print(round(gamma2, 2))
print(round(R, 2))
print(round(Rm, 2))
print(round(mm, 2))
print(round(zv1, 2))

traps: Using the actual tooth count z in the Lewis form factor instead of the virtual tooth count z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos γ.
Taking the tangential load at the outer radius instead of the mean radius. At the same torque, the outer radius gives a smaller force, so the design is unsafe.
Adding cone angles to 180° instead of to the shaft angle. For a 90° pair, γ<sub>1</sub> + γ<sub>2</sub> = 90°.
Using the large-end module m in the Lewis equation when the load acts at the mean section. Use m<sub>m</sub> = m R<sub>m</sub>/R.
Making the face width larger than R/3. The tooth becomes stiff at one end and lightly loaded at the other, so the load is not shared as assumed.

quiz.q: For a 90° bevel pair, write the relation between the pinion cone angle γ<sub>1</sub> and the tooth numbers.
quiz.a: tan γ<sub>1</sub> = z<sub>1</sub>/z<sub>2</sub>, and γ<sub>2</sub> = 90° − γ<sub>1</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is the Lewis form factor read for z<sub>v</sub> rather than for z?
quiz.a: The back cone unrolls into a plane and the bevel tooth has the shape of a spur tooth on a larger pitch circle. That equivalent spur gear has z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos γ teeth, so its form factor matches the actual tooth shape.

quiz.q: A 90° pair has z<sub>1</sub> = 18, z<sub>2</sub> = 36 and m = 5 mm. Find γ<sub>1</sub> and R.
A designer increases face width from R/4 to R/2. Explain the effect on load sharing and on the Lewis check.
quiz.a: The tooth is stiffer at the large end and less stiff at the small end. Load shifts to the large end, so the assumed uniform load at the mean section is no longer valid. The Lewis check with the mean module becomes optimistic, and contact near the outer end may fail. Keep b ≤ R/3.

quiz.q: Define cone distance R and mean module m<sub>m</sub>.
quiz.a: R is the slant length from the pitch cone apex to the large end. m<sub>m</sub> is the module at the mean section, m<sub>m</sub> = m R<sub>m</sub>/R, where R<sub>m</sub> = R − b/2.

quiz.q: Why does a straight bevel pinion produce axial thrust?
quiz.a: The normal force resolves into the tangential part W<sub>t</sub> and a part W<sub>t</sub> tan φ lying in the axial plane, the plane through the contact point that contains the shaft axis. Resolving that second part gives axial W<sub>t</sub> tan φ sin γ and radial W<sub>t</sub> tan φ cos γ.

quiz.q: W<sub>t</sub> = 2000 N, φ = 20° and γ = 26.57°. Find the axial thrust on the pinion.
A student uses the outer radius R to compute W<sub>t</sub> from torque. Is the design safe or unsafe? Explain.
quiz.a: Unsafe. For the same torque, W<sub>t</sub> = T/r gives a smaller force at the larger radius. The real load acts near the mean radius, where r is smaller, so the true W<sub>t</sub> is larger. The bending stress is underpredicted.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, straight bevel gears are cut on mechanical or CNC generators, and the tooth form is checked for contact pattern under light load. Spiral bevel and hypoid sets dominate vehicle differentials because they run quieter and allow an offset axis. Search next for Gleason bevel gear design, ISO 10300 bevel gear rating, and hypoid offset. Bearing and housing deflection often set the real limit before bending strength does.
